threads.thread_goal: Align on current workflow, main pain points and pilot scope for one aisle.

messages.text:
Kicking off the Store Backroom-to-Shelf Replenishment Optimisation Pilot for project_pack_ref: Store Backroom-to-Shelf Replenishment Optimisation Pilot.
For this thread, can we map how things work today from backroom to shelf for one aisle, and surface the main pain points?
I will start drafting the current workflow for T1 and capture it in A1, but I need your input:
- Which aisle do you think is the best candidate for the pilot?
- For that aisle, how do steps usually run today from truck unloading, backroom, then onto shelves?
Please describe your part of the flow in short steps, including any delays or safety issues you see regularly.

From the mover side, for the chilled food aisle, the usual flow is:
- Truck arrives, we shunt inbound loads to the back door.
- I unload pallets with the forklift and park them in the backroom near the chiller.
- I roughly group pallets by temperature and weight, but not always by aisle.
- When shelf fillers are ready, I move trolleys to the aisle, trying not to block customers.
Pain points:
- We sometimes stack heavy boxes on top of lighter ones when it is busy.
- Backroom gets crowded, so it is hard to find the right pallet quickly.
- Cleaning around the loading area is not always done before the next truck.
If we pick the chilled aisle, we need to be strict on safety and hygiene.

From the shelf side, for ambient groceries (pasta, tins, sauces), the flow is:
- I get a trolley that is already mixed from different aisles.
- I park it at the end of the aisle and start filling from the middle, not always from one end.
- I rotate stock when I remember, but when it is busy I just fill gaps.
- Labels and prices are checked only when a customer points out an issue or when we do a promo change.
Pain points:
- Mixed trolleys mean I walk a lot between aisles.
- Sometimes I find damaged packaging on the trolley and I am not sure where to log it.
- Aisle can be blocked when cleaning and filling happen at the same time.
For a pilot aisle, ambient groceries might be easier than chilled to start with.

From the office side, I see the process mainly through delivery notes and stock records:
- I receive the delivery paperwork and check counts against the system.
- I do not always know exactly when items reach the shelf, so stock on hand can look correct even if the shelf is empty.
- For price accuracy, I rely on planned label changes, not on what actually happens on the shelf.
Pain points:
- Hard to link a stock discrepancy to a specific step in the backroom-to-shelf flow.
- No simple way to log small incidents like one damaged case or a missing tray.
For T1 and later T6, I can help document these handoffs in A1 and A6 once we agree on the pilot aisle.

Adding what I see when I help on the floor:
- For the snacks and drinks aisle, trolleys arrive already half picked from other aisles.
- We sometimes leave half-empty boxes in the backroom because we are not sure if they belong to the pilot aisle or another one.
- When customers ask for an item that is not on the shelf, I have to go to the back and search, which takes time.
Pain points:
- No clear visual sign in the backroom for which pallet or box is for which aisle.
- I do not have a simple sheet yet to note when we find missing or damaged items.
This might be relevant when we set up A5 and A7 later, but for now it affects how we map T1.

Thanks all, this is helpful.
To choose the pilot aisle for D1, we need something with:
- Manageable safety risk for a first run.
- Clear stock rotation needs.
- Enough volume to see impact within 21 days.
We have chilled, ambient groceries, and snacks/drinks as options from your comments. My first thought is ambient groceries: less temperature risk than chilled, but still strong rotation and label checks.
Any strong objections to using the main ambient grocery aisle as the pilot scope, focusing on pasta, tins, and sauces as the initial product categories?

No objection from me. Ambient groceries are easier from a loading point of view.
For that aisle today:
- I usually bring mixed pallets that include ambient plus other stuff.
- I do not plan the sequence by aisle, more by what is on top of the pallet.
If we pick that aisle, I can help later on T2 to define a better loading and movement sequence in A2 so that trolleys are grouped by that aisle first.

I support using the main ambient grocery aisle.
It is busy enough that we will see if the new routine works, but we do not have the same strict temperature timing as chilled.
From my side, I can document the current shelf routine for that aisle for T4 and later help compare it with the new routine in A4.

Ambient groceries work for me as well.
From a records point of view, it is easier to track stock accuracy there than in chilled, because we have fewer short-dated items.
I will update the draft of A1 so that T1 focuses on the main ambient grocery aisle and those three product categories.
Once we confirm D1, I can also start sketching T6 for that aisle in A6.

I am ok with the ambient grocery aisle too.
One question: do we include snacks and drinks in the same pilot, or keep it to pasta, tins, and sauces only at first?
If we keep it narrower, it might be easier for me to help track incidents in A7 and later summarise them for T11.

Good point. For the first run, I suggest we limit the pilot scope to the main ambient grocery aisle, and within that aisle to pasta, tins, and sauces only.
We can add snacks and drinks later if the pilot goes well.
Unless anyone disagrees by this afternoon, I will record D1 as:
- Pilot aisle: main ambient grocery aisle.
- Product categories: pasta, tins, sauces.

Works for me. Narrow scope will help us test the loading sequence properly.
I will pay attention to how we currently move those three categories so we have a clear before picture for T2 and T7 later.

Agreed on that scope.
I will note down how often we see gaps or mispriced items in that aisle this week so we can compare once A4 and the new routine for T4 and T8 are in place.

No objections from me.
I will finalise the current-state map in A1 for T1 with that aisle and those categories.
Next question is timing: we have a 21-day window. I suggest we:
- Use 3 days to finish mapping and prep (A1, A6).
- Run the pilot for one full stock cycle of 14 days.
- Keep a few days at the end for T11 and A8.
Does that sound realistic from the floor side?

From the loading side, that timing is ok.
If we start the pilot on Monday next week, that gives us the rest of this week to map and adjust without changing the live process too much.
Two delivery days per week for that aisle should be enough to see if the new sequence works.

Monday start works for me too.
For the shelf routine, I would like at least a couple of days before that to walk through the current steps and note where we skip rotation or label checks.
If we lock the start date as next Monday and run for 14 days, we can still fit within the 21-day limit.

I am fine with that plan.
I just want to confirm: do we count the 14 days as calendar days or only days when we have deliveries for that aisle?
For T5 and A5 later, it might be easier if we say calendar days so we have a daily habit of updating the tracking sheet.

Good catch. I suggest we define the pilot duration as 14 calendar days, starting next Monday, with daily tracking even on lighter days.
That keeps us clearly within the 21-day window and makes T5 and A5 easier to manage.
I will record D2 as:
- Pilot start date: next Monday.
- Pilot duration: 14 calendar days.
I will also record D1 as agreed earlier:
- Pilot aisle: main ambient grocery aisle.
- Product categories: pasta, tins, sauces.
I will share a short summary in A6 once I update T6 with this scope and timing.

Thanks, I will align T1 and A1 with that scope and timing and start sketching the shift allocation in A6 for T6.
I will also note in the doc that we are focusing on pasta, tins, and sauces only for this first cycle.

threads.thread_goal: Define and validate the new loading, movement and shelf routines.

messages.text:
Following up on the scope we agreed for the ambient grocery aisle, I have pulled together a first draft of:
- A2: standard loading and movement sequence for pasta, tins, and sauces (T2).
- A4: shelf replenishment routine for that aisle (T4).
Summary of the proposal:
Loading and movement (A2, T2):
- Group pallets in the backroom by aisle, then by weight.
- Build trolleys dedicated to the pilot aisle only, in the order we want to fill the shelves.
- Move one trolley at a time to avoid blocking aisles.
Shelf routine (A4, T4):
- Start at one end of the aisle and work through in order.
- Always rotate stock, checking dates as you go.
- Check labels and prices as part of the same pass.
Please review and comment, especially on safety, walking distance, and how realistic this is during busy times.

On the loading side, the draft in A2 makes sense overall.
A few details from what I see today:
- When we group pallets by aisle, we need to watch weight distribution so heavy tins stay low and lighter pasta goes higher.
- For dangerous goods, we do not have many in this aisle, but we still need to avoid stacking cleaning products above food if they share a pallet.
- Moving one trolley at a time is safer, but we might need two during quiet hours to keep up.
For T2, I suggest we add:
- A simple rule for stacking order on the trolley.
- A note to check the floor is clean and dry before moving the trolley, linking to T10 so cleaning does not clash with loading.

On the shelf routine in A4:
- Starting at one end and working through in order will help me avoid missing sections.
- Doing rotation and label checks in the same pass is efficient, but we need to be clear what to do if we find a mispriced item.
- For dates, I suggest we define a quick rule, like always bring older stock to the front and remove anything past date immediately.
For T4, could we add:
- A short step for what to do with damaged or out-of-date items (probably link to A7 later).
- A reminder to keep the aisle clear for customers while filling, maybe by limiting how many boxes we open at once.

From the records side, I like that A2 and A4 both follow a clear order.
A couple of questions:
- For A2, can we note at which point we update any internal notes so that stock in the system does not look full while the trolley is still in the backroom?
- For A4, when we change labels or prices, should we log anything in A5 or just correct it on the spot?
This will affect how we design T5 and T11 later, so I want to make sure the routine gives us enough data without slowing you down too much.

I went through the drafts as well.
On A2:
- Maybe we can add a simple visual mark on trolleys for the pilot aisle so we do not mix them with others.
- For T10, we should note that cleaning of that aisle floor happens either just before or just after the trolley run, not during.
On A4:
- Could we include a quick check at the end of the run to look down the aisle and confirm there are no obvious gaps or messy sections?
That would help when we later fill in A5 for shelf condition.

Thanks for the detailed feedback.
I will update A2 to include:
- Clear stacking rules: heavy tins at the bottom, lighter pasta above, no cleaning products above food.
- A step to check the floor is clean and dry before moving the trolley, and a note to coordinate with cleaning as part of T10.
On the number of trolleys, we can define:
- One trolley at a time as the default.
- Two trolleys allowed during quiet hours if the aisle is not blocked.
I will mark these as version 2 of the draft for T2.

For A4, I will add:
- A step for damaged or out-of-date items: remove from shelf, place in a designated crate, and log in A7.
- A reminder to open only a limited number of boxes at a time to keep the aisle clear.
For mispriced items, I suggest:
- Correct the label immediately if you can.
- If you cannot, note it in A5 under mispriced items so we can follow up.
Does that fit with how you usually work on the aisle?

Yes, that fits.
Having a clear crate for damaged or out-of-date items and logging them in A7 will make it easier to remember.
I like the idea of noting mispriced items in A5 when we cannot fix them on the spot.
For T4, could we also specify how long a full pass of the aisle should take roughly, so we know if we are falling behind during the pilot?

The updated A2 sounds workable.
On the visual mark for trolleys that 300804 mentioned, we could:
- Use a coloured tag for the pilot aisle.
- Note in T2 that only tagged trolleys follow the new sequence.
For T7, when we pilot the sequence on two delivery days, I can log any delays or issues in A7 so we can refine further.

On your questions:
- For A2, I suggest we say that stock is considered on shelf once the trolley enters the aisle and filling starts, not when it leaves the backroom. That way, we can align system updates with that moment.
- For A4, I would log only repeated label issues in A5. One-off corrections can just be fixed on the spot.
I can add a short note about this in A5 as part of T5 so everyone knows what to record.

That helps, thanks.
I will make sure A5 has a simple field for repeated label issues and another for general shelf condition.
For T11 later, it will be useful to see how many of those we get before and after the new routines.

On timing for T4, based on your usual pace, would 45 to 60 minutes for a full pass of the pilot categories sound reasonable during normal traffic?
We can note that as a guideline in A4, and during T8 we can see if that holds in practice.
If everyone is comfortable with the updated A2 and A4, I would like to move towards confirming them for the pilot.

Yes, 45 to 60 minutes for a full pass of pasta, tins, and sauces sounds realistic on a normal day.
On very busy days it might stretch a bit, but having that range in A4 will help us see when we are really behind.
I am comfortable using the updated A4 for the pilot.

I am ok with the updated A2 as well.
The stacking rules, floor check, and trolley tagging are clear enough for us to follow on shift.
For T7, I will make sure we apply the full sequence on at least two delivery days and note any problems in A7.

From my side, both A2 and A4 look ready to use for the pilot.
I will just double-check that the steps line up with the shift allocation in A6 so we do not overload any one person.
Once we confirm, I will reference them in the brief for the team.

Great, thanks all.
I will record D3 and D4 as follows:
D3: We approve the standard loading and movement sequence in A2 for the pilot aisle, including stacking rules, floor checks, trolley tagging, and coordination with cleaning (T2, T10). This sequence will be piloted on at least two delivery days as part of T7.
D4: We approve the shelf replenishment routine in A4 for the pilot aisle, including full-pass order, rotation and date checks, label handling, damaged and out-of-date item handling via A7, and the target time range for a full pass (T4, T8).
I will update A2 and A4 to mark them as pilot-ready and share a short summary in the channel.

threads.thread_goal: Lock in safety, hygiene and incident logging practices for the pilot.

messages.text:
For the next step of the pilot, I have drafted:
- A3: safety and hygiene checklist for movers and shelf fillers (T3).
- A7: incident and exception log for damaged, missing, or unsafe items (T9).
Key points in A3:
- Lifting and stacking checks for movers.
- Food safety and date checks for shelf fillers.
- Quick cleaning checks around the aisle and backroom.
Key fields in A7:
- Date, time, location (backroom or aisle).
- Type of issue (damaged, missing, unsafe, delay).
- Short description and what was done.
Please review and comment so we can confirm what everyone must do on shift and when to fill in A7.

Looking at A3 from the mover side:
- The lifting checks are clear: bend knees, keep load close, do not twist.
- For stacking, it says heavy at the bottom and no overhanging boxes, which matches what we discussed in A2.
- There is a line about dangerous goods, but we do not have many in this aisle. Maybe we just remind people not to stack cleaning products above food.
For A7, I would log:
- Any time a pallet or trolley is unstable.
- Any near-miss where a box almost falls.
Do we want those near-misses in A7 as well, or only actual incidents?

From the shelf side, A3 covers the basics:
- Check dates and rotate stock.
- Do not place damaged or leaking items on the shelf.
- Keep the aisle clear and clean.
I have two questions:
- For food hygiene, should we include a quick hand hygiene reminder before handling open packaging?
- For A7, when I find an out-of-date item, do I log every single one or only if we find a lot at once?

I checked A3 and A7 as well.
On A3:
- It might help to group the checks by role: one section for movers, one for shelf fillers, so people can scan quickly.
- Maybe we can add a small box to tick at the start and end of the shift, rather than for every single action.
On A7:
- The fields look simple enough.
- Could we add a checkbox for whether the issue affected customers (for example, blocked aisle or missing product on shelf)?
That would help when we summarise incidents later for T11.

From an admin point of view, A3 and A7 look like they can fit on one page each, which is good.
We also need to think about T12: validating that the new process meets safety and hygiene requirements.
For that, the health and safety officer will want to see:
- That A3 is used consistently for at least a week.
- That A7 is filled in for relevant incidents.
So we should be clear in this thread about when exactly staff must use A3 and A7 during the pilot.

On near-misses: I suggest we do log them in A7, but maybe with a simple tag so we can filter later.
That way, we can see patterns without making the form too heavy.
I will add a field in A7 for 'incident' vs 'near-miss'.
On dangerous goods, I will simplify the wording in A3 for this aisle to focus on not stacking cleaning products above food, as you suggest.

For your questions:
- Yes, we should add a short hand hygiene reminder in A3, especially before handling any open or damaged packaging.
- For out-of-date items, I propose we log them in A7 only when we find more than a small number at once, for example more than three of the same product or a full case.
Single items can just be removed and handled as usual.
I will update A3 and A7 accordingly.

That works for me.
Logging near-misses in A7 with a tag is simple enough, and it will help us spot if we have repeated issues with stacking or trolley movement.
For T9, we should probably include a short example in the briefing so people know what counts as a near-miss.

Thanks, that clarifies it.
I like the idea of logging only bigger groups of out-of-date items in A7.
For A3, grouping checks by role as 300804 suggested would help me quickly see what I need to do at the start of the shift.
Maybe we can have a small tick box for 'start of shift' and 'end of shift' checks for shelf fillers.

On the checkbox for customer impact in A7, I can help format that so it is easy to tick.
For T9, we might also want a short line at the top of A7 that says when to fill it in, for example:
- When there is damage, missing stock, unsafe situation, delay, or repeated out-of-date items.
That way, people do not have to guess.

I will reformat A3 so it has two sections:
- Movers: lifting, stacking, trolley movement, backroom cleanliness.
- Shelf fillers: rotation, date checks, damaged items, aisle cleanliness, hand hygiene.
Each section will have a small start-of-shift and end-of-shift tick box.
For A7, I will add the customer impact checkbox and the short line at the top about when to use the form, as you and 300804 suggested.

On when to use A3 and A7 during the pilot, here is a proposal:
A3 (T3, T12):
- Each mover and shelf filler in the pilot uses A3 at the start and end of every shift that touches the pilot aisle.
- Spot checks by the supervisor once per day.
A7 (T9):
- Filled in whenever there is a relevant incident or near-miss as defined at the top of the form.
- At least three sample entries during the pilot to prove the process works.
If we agree on this, it should give the health and safety officer enough evidence for T12.

I can work with that.
Using A3 at the start and end of the shift is manageable, and logging incidents and near-misses in A7 as they happen is fine.
We just need to make sure the forms are easy to reach in the backroom and near the aisle.

Agreed from my side too.
Start and end of shift checks with A3 are clear, and I can fill in A7 when I find bigger groups of out-of-date items, damaged goods, or if the aisle is blocked.
For T12, I will keep my completed A3 sheets together so they are easy to review at the end of the week.

I am ok with that plan.
I can help collect A7 forms at the end of each day and make sure they are stored in one place.
That will make it easier later when we summarise incidents for T11 and A8.

Sounds good.
I will finalise A3 and A7 with the changes we discussed and mark them as ready for the pilot.
I will also prepare a short briefing note for T3 and T9 so everyone knows how to use them from day one.

Based on the discussion, I will record:
D5: We confirm the final version of the safety and hygiene checklist in A3 for the pilot. Movers and shelf fillers will complete it at the start and end of each shift that touches the pilot aisle, with daily spot checks. This supports T3 and T12.
D6: We agree that the incident and exception log in A7 will be filled in for incidents and near-misses as defined on the form, including damage, missing stock, unsafe situations, delays, and repeated out-of-date items. At least three sample entries will be recorded during the pilot as part of T9.
I will share these points with the health and safety officer for awareness.

threads.thread_goal: Coordinate daily execution, tracking and quick fixes during the pilot.

messages.text:
Pilot day 1 for the ambient grocery aisle.
For this thread, let us use it as our daily async check-in:
- What you did on the pilot aisle.
- Any issues or incidents (and whether they are in A7).
- Plan for the next shift.
Reminder:
- Use A2 and A4 as the standard routines.
- Use A3 and A7 for safety, hygiene, and incidents.
- A5 is our stock accuracy and shelf condition tracking sheet (T5).
We also need to agree how often we update A5 and share a quick status here for D7.

Day shift update from loading side:
- Used A2 for the first delivery: grouped pallets by aisle and built a dedicated trolley for pasta and tins.
- Checked floor was clean before moving the trolley and used the coloured tag.
- Only one trolley in the aisle at a time.
Issues:
- One box of tins had a slightly crushed corner but product inside looked fine. I set it aside and told the shelf filler.
- No near-misses or unstable trolleys.
I did not log anything in A7 yet because the box was still usable. Next time should I log that as minor damage or only if we remove items?

Shelf side, first pass:
- Followed A4 from one end of the aisle to the other for pasta and tins.
- Rotated stock and checked dates; found two out-of-date tins, removed them and put them in the crate.
- Corrected one mispriced label on pasta.
I updated A5 for:
- Shelf gaps: none.
- Mispriced items: one corrected on the spot.
- Shelf condition: tidy.
I did not log the two out-of-date tins in A7 because it was only two of one product. Let me know if that is ok.

Thanks for the updates.
On the questions:
- For the slightly crushed box that is still usable, I would not log it in A7 unless we remove product or it creates a safety risk.
- For the two out-of-date tins, your approach is correct: remove them, no need to log in A7 unless we see a bigger group.
I have added today s entries to A5 based on your notes.
For T5, we need to decide how often we update A5: my suggestion is once per shift (day and evening) so we have two entries per day.

Admin update:
- I created today s tab in A5 and copied over the fields for counts, gaps, mispricing, and shelf condition.
- I also set up a simple place to store A7 forms at the back of the aisle.
For D7, I like the idea of updating A5 once per shift and posting a short status here at shift change.
That would give us:
- Day shift update.
- Evening shift update.
Does that feel manageable for you on the floor?

Once per shift for A5 sounds fine from my side.
I can add a short note on stock arriving and any delays or blocked aisles.
For A7, I had one small delay today when another trolley blocked the backroom door for a few minutes. I will log that as a minor delay so we can see if it repeats.

I can handle one A5 update per shift as well.
At the end of my pass, I will:
- Check for gaps and mispriced items.
- Note shelf condition.
- Mention any customer impact, like if the aisle was blocked.
Today there was one short moment when a customer had to walk around the trolley, but the aisle was not fully blocked, so I did not log it in A7.

Good, sounds like once per shift for A5 is acceptable.
For D7, I propose we define our rhythm as:
- A5 updated twice per day: once at the end of the day shift, once at the end of the evening shift.
- Short status post in this thread at each shift change with what was done, issues, and plan for next shift.
If everyone agrees, we can lock that in and keep using this pattern for the rest of the pilot.

I am ok with that rhythm.
I will post a short update here at the end of each day shift and make sure A5 is filled in from the loading side.

Works for me too.
I will handle the evening shift updates for A5 and post here with any shelf issues or incidents logged in A7.

Agreed.
I will keep an eye on A5 to make sure both shifts are updating it and that we capture enough detail for T11 later.
I will also do a quick end-of-day incident summary based on A7 entries.

I am aligned as well.
I will help check that A5 is filled in twice a day and that A7 forms are collected and stored.
If we see that updates are slipping, I will flag it here so we can adjust.

Thanks all.
I will record D7 as:
- A5 will be updated twice per day, at the end of the day and evening shifts.
- Each shift will post a short status in this thread at shift change, including what was done, issues, and plan for the next shift.
This will be our standard rhythm for the rest of the pilot.

End of day shift, day 2 update:
- Used A2 for one more delivery, no issues with stacking or trolley movement.
- Logged one minor delay in A7 when cleaning was still finishing in the aisle; we waited a few minutes before entering.
Plan for next shift:
- Same loading sequence, try to reduce waiting time by checking cleaning schedule (T10).

End of evening shift, day 2 update:
- Followed A4 for pasta, tins, and sauces.
- Found one small gap in sauces; filled it from the backroom stock.
- No mispriced items today.
- Logged in A5: one gap resolved, shelf condition good.
No incidents to add to A7.
Plan for tomorrow evening: focus on checking labels more closely on the sauces section.

End-of-day summary:
- A5 has both day and evening entries for day 2.
- A7 has two minor delays logged so far, no major incidents.
I will keep tracking this pattern through the week so we have enough data for T11 and A8.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results and agree on next steps and improvements.

messages.text:
We have reached the end of the 14-day pilot for the ambient grocery aisle.
I have pulled together a first summary in A8 based on:
- A5: stock accuracy and shelf condition tracking.
- A7: incident and exception log.
- Notes from this channel.
Headline results:
- Shelf gaps reduced compared to the first days.
- Fewer mispriced items after the first week.
- A small number of minor delays and near-misses, no major safety incidents.
I have also drafted three improvement proposals in T11.
Let us review the results and decide which process changes to keep and whether to extend the pilot to more aisles for D8.

From the loading side, looking back at the pilot:
- The sequence in A2 worked well on both delivery days we used for T7.
- Trolley tagging and stacking rules reduced the time spent searching for the right boxes.
- Most delays logged in A7 were due to cleaning overlap or other trolleys blocking the backroom door.
If we keep this process, I would suggest:
- Making the trolley tagging permanent for this aisle.
- Tightening coordination with cleaning as part of T10 so we avoid the small delays we saw.

From the shelf side:
- Following A4 made it easier to avoid missing sections; I noticed fewer surprise gaps after the first week.
- Date checks caught a few groups of out-of-date tins early; we logged the bigger ones in A7.
- Label checks reduced mispriced items; A5 shows fewer repeated label issues in the second week.
If we extend the process, I would keep:
- The full-pass routine with rotation and label checks.
- The damaged and out-of-date item handling via A7.
We might need to adjust the target time for a full pass on very busy days, but overall it felt workable.

Looking at A5 and A7 together:
- A5 shows that shelf condition ratings improved from 'ok' to 'good' or 'very good' on most days after day 4.
- Mispriced items dropped from a few per day to almost none by the end.
- A7 has several minor delays and a few near-misses, but no serious incidents.
For T11, the three improvement proposals I see are:
1) Keep the dedicated trolley and tagging for the pilot aisle.
2) Keep the full-pass shelf routine with rotation and label checks.
3) Adjust cleaning schedules (T10) to avoid overlap with trolley movement.
I am interested in your view on whether we should extend this to snacks and drinks next.

From an admin and coordination angle:
- A3 and A7 usage was consistent enough for the health and safety officer to review; they were satisfied that T12 is met for this pilot.
- A5 updates twice per day worked, though a few evening entries were shorter than ideal.
- A6 shift allocation seemed balanced; no one role was overloaded.
If we extend, we should:
- Keep the same daily rhythm for A5 and channel updates.
- Revisit A6 to include any new aisles.
I am leaning towards extending the process to one more aisle, but I want to hear if there were any hidden issues on the floor first.

No hidden issues from my side.
The only thing to watch if we extend to snacks and drinks is that those pallets can be heavier and more mixed.
